title: Yesterday
job: Past tense — the first big divergence
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The past is a SECOND STEM, learned per verb, with regular endings on it. veniō gives vēnī, legō gives lēgī, scrībō gives scrīpsī, habeō gives habuī, sum gives fuī. The endings are predictable; the stems are not, which is why a dictionary lists a third shape for every verb.

One Latin past covers two English ones. Lēgī is 'I read' and 'I have read', and there is nothing to choose between. English makes you decide whether the action is finished or connected to now; Latin does not ask.

There is no helper verb anywhere in it. English builds 'I have read' out of 'have' plus a participle, and Latin has habeō and does NOT use it here — lēgī is one word. A learner who reaches for habeō to make a past tense has built a sentence about possession.

The whole difference between venit and vēnit is one bar. venit is 'he comes' (M4) and vēnit is 'he came' (here), and the same trick runs through the module: the long vowel IS the tense. Write the bar or you have written the wrong tense, and a Roman hears the length the way you hear 'ship' against 'sheep'.

The past does NOT carry the speaker's gender. Vēnī is the same word whoever says it — which is worth saying because a Latin sentence has carried gender since M1. Where gender lands is after fuī: a man says Rōmānus fuī and a woman Rōmāna fuī, because the adjective describes the person and the verb does not.

The bar on the end matters as much as the one inside. Vēnī is 'I came' and vēnit is 'he came' — the long ī is the person. Two long vowels in one short word, doing two different jobs, is ordinary in this tense.

'I was reading' and 'I used to read' are NOT this tense. Latin has a separate past for them and this course does not teach it yet — every English past that means a habit or an unfinished action waits for a later level. Here, everything is a completed event: Herī vēnī.

words.note: 'Yesterday', and it never changes shape — an adverb like cotīdiē. Its final ī is long, so the stress stays on the first syllable: HE-rī.
'I came' — the past of M4's veniō, built on a different stem: vēnī 'I came', vēnit 'he/she came'. Both bars matter; the first is the tense and the second the person.

sentences.trap: Two words, and one of them is the whole past tense with its subject inside it. English needs three — 'I came yesterday' — and two of them do work Latin does with endings.
sentences.sound: HE-rī VAY-nee. Both vowels of vēnī are long: hold the ē and hold the ī. Said next to M4's VEN-it, the difference is unmistakable — and that is the point of the bar.

variations.changed: the final bar goes and the person changes; the tense does not
the time word dropped — the tense is in the verb, not in herī
negated, with nōn in front and no helper to build

mistake.why: The first bar dropped, which takes the tense with it. venī with a short e is the command 'come!', so the sentence has turned from a report into an order — and nothing on the page except that bar says which you meant.

sentences.mnemonic: Long ē, past. Short e, present. The bar is the tense.

words.note: A Roman woman's given name, said YOO-li-a. Spelled with an i because Latin has no letter j at all.
'Yesterday', and it never changes shape — an adverb like cotīdiē. Its final ī is long, so the stress stays on the first syllable: HE-rī.
'I came' — the past of M4's veniō, built on a different stem: vēnī 'I came', vēnit 'he/she came'. The bar inside is the tense; without it this is 'she comes'.

sentences.trap: Put this beside M4's Iūlia cotīdiē venit and the only difference on the page is one bar. That bar is the entire past tense, and it is why this course marks every long vowel rather than leaving them to be guessed.
sentences.sound: YOO-li-a HE-rī VAY-nit. Hold the ē. Then say M4's VEN-it immediately afterwards and hear that they are two different words.

variations.changed: a man instead, and the verb does not move — the past carries no gender
back to the present, which is M4's sentence and differs by one bar
negated, with no 'did' to build

mistake.why: The bar dropped, so the sentence says Julia comes yesterday — a present tense with a past time word, which is nonsense in Latin as it is in English. This is the error the whole orthography exists to make visible.

sentences.mnemonic: herī wants a bar on the verb.

words.note: 'Book': liber as the subject, librum as the object, librī for more than one. The e drops out as soon as an ending is added.
'I read' in the past — the second stem of M4's legō, with its e lengthened: lēgī 'I read', lēgit 'he read'. It also covers 'I have read'.

sentences.trap: One Latin word covers 'I read', 'I have read' and 'I did read'. English makes you choose between them and Latin does not offer the choice — so there is nothing here to get wrong except the stem.
sentences.sound: LI-brum LAY-gee. Both vowels of lēgī are long. Beside M4's LE-git the past is audibly slower, which is exactly how a Roman told them apart.

variations.changed: the person moves; the long e of the stem stays
a time word added, which the tense did not need
a different thing read, still in the object shape

mistake.why: 'I have read' assembled out of habeō and a participle, the way English builds it. Latin's lēgī already means that, and this construction says something closer to 'I possess a book that has been read'.

sentences.usage: Said about anything you finished reading.
sentences.mnemonic: legō becomes lēgī: the vowel stretches and the tense moves.

words.note: 'Letter' — the written kind. epistula as the subject, epistulam as the object. English kept it in 'epistle'.
'I wrote' — the second stem of M4's scrībō, and the b has become ps: scrīpsī, scrīpsit 'he wrote'. English keeps that ps in 'script'.

sentences.trap: The b of scrībō turned into ps. A past stem is not the present with a suffix — it can change the consonants as well as the vowel, which is why it has to be learned as a separate word.
sentences.sound: e-PIS-tu-lam SCRIP-see. The ī of scrīpsī is long and stressed; the final ī is long too.

variations.changed: the person moves on the same stem
a time word added

variations.cue: I did not write a letter.
variations.changed: negated, and English's 'did' has nothing to become

mistake.why: The past built by putting the ending straight onto the present stem. It does not work: the stem itself changes, and scrībō's past is scrīpsī — there is no rule to derive it from, only the dictionary.

sentences.usage: Said about correspondence you have finished.
sentences.mnemonic: scrībō, scrīpsī — the b becomes the ps of 'script'.

words.note: 'Roman', bending for the person it describes: Rōmānus of a man, Rōmāna of a woman, Rōmānī of more than one. Both ō and ā are long.
'I was' — the past of sum, and it shares no letters with it at all: fuī, fuit 'he was'. The most irregular verb in the language is irregular here too.

sentences.trap: The gender is on the adjective and not on the verb. fuī is the same word whoever says it, and a woman changes Rōmānus to Rōmāna and leaves fuī alone — which is the opposite of what several other languages do.
sentences.sound: ro-MA-nus FU-ee. fuī is two syllables, FU-ee, and the final ī is long.

variations.changed: the adjective takes her gender and the verb does not move
the person moves, on a stem that looks nothing like sum
a noun instead of an adjective, doing the same job

mistake.why: Both tenses of the same verb in one sentence, because English's 'was' looks like it needs 'be' inside it. fuī is the whole past of sum, so the sentence has two verbs and no room for the second.

sentences.usage: Said about what you used to be — though for a lasting state, a later level has a better tense.
sentences.mnemonic: sum and fuī are one verb with two unrelated halves.

words.note: 'Yesterday', and it never changes shape — an adverb like cotīdiē. Its final ī is long, so the stress stays on the first syllable: HE-rī.
'Water': aqua as the subject, aquam as the object, aquā as the thing needed. Three shapes of one word.
'I had' — the past of M3's habeō, with a u in the stem: habuī, habuit 'he had'. This is the verb for possessing, never a helper for building other pasts.

sentences.trap: habuī is 'I had' and nothing else. It is not the piece English uses to build 'I have read' — Latin's past needs no helper, so habeō and habuī only ever talk about possession.
sentences.sound: HE-rī A-quam ha-BU-ee. habuī is three syllables with the stress in the middle.

variations.changed: the person moves on the same u-stem
a different thing had
negated, with no 'did' to supply

mistake.why: The other past tense, the one this course has not taught. habēbam is 'I was having / I used to have' and it is a different form for a different job — L4 opens it, and reaching for it here writes a tense the learner cannot yet use correctly.

sentences.usage: Said about what you had at some point.
sentences.mnemonic: habeō becomes habuī: the e gives way to a u.

words.note: A Roman man's given name, with a genuinely long ā: MAR-cus. A name takes endings like any other noun — Mārcō is 'to Marcus'.
'Yesterday', and it never changes shape — an adverb like cotīdiē. Its final ī is long, so the stress stays on the first syllable: HE-rī.
'I read' in the past — the second stem of M4's legō, with its e lengthened: lēgī 'I read', lēgit 'he read'. The bar is the tense: legit is 'he reads'.

sentences.trap: lēgit against M4's legit is the same trap as vēnit against venit, on a different verb. English does the same thing with 'read' and 'read' and gives you no spelling to help; Latin gives you the bar, and that is why it is written.
sentences.sound: MAR-cus HE-rī LAY-git. Hold the ē. M4's legit is LEG-it, short and quick.

variations.changed: an object added and the time word dropped
the present with a past time word — deliberately broken, to show what one bar carries
a woman instead, and the verb does not move

mistake.why: The bar missing, so the tense is present and the time word is past. This is the same sentence as the third variation above, which is there on purpose: the module wants you to see it once as a demonstration and once as an error.

sentences.usage: Said about what somebody did yesterday.
sentences.mnemonic: legit reads, lēgit read. The bar is the past.

words.note: 'Not', and it goes straight in front of the verb. Nothing corresponds to English 'did not': there is no helper to hang the negative on in any tense.
'I came' — the past of M4's veniō, built on a different stem: vēnī 'I came', vēnit 'he/she came'. Both bars matter; the first is the tense and the second the person.

sentences.trap: English's 'did' has nothing to become. It exists only to carry the tense and the negative, and Latin's verb carries both itself — so a two-word English past becomes a two-word Latin sentence with nothing in common.
sentences.sound: NON VAY-nee. Three long vowels in two short words, which makes a flat, deliberate sound.

variations.changed: the person moves; nōn does not
a time word in front of the negative
a different verb under the same negative

mistake.why: A past negative assembled out of a helper and an infinitive, on the model of 'did not come'. Every piece is a real Latin word and the whole means roughly 'I did not possess to come' — which is why the module's rule says nōn sits on the verb and stops.

sentences.usage: Said when you are explaining an absence.
sentences.mnemonic: nōn plus the past verb. Nothing else is needed.

sentences.cue: I was a student. (a woman speaking)

mistake.why: A feminine ending invented for the verb, because the noun has one. Latin verbs in this tense do not carry gender at all — fuī is the whole word, and adding to it produces nothing.

sentences.usage: Said about what you used to do.
sentences.mnemonic: The noun knows your gender. The verb does not.
